title: Atom economy; Practical techniques and uncertainties
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM10#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM10#N.3, PR01a#N.5, AM10#N.5, PR01a#N.10, AM10#N.9, PR01a#N.12, PR01a#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Accuracy
items.clue: How close a result is to the true value.

items.label: Precision
items.clue: How close repeat readings are to each other.

items.label: Random error
items.clue: Makes readings scatter either way; repeats and a mean reduce its effect.

items.label: Atom economy
items.clue: Percentage of the total mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product.

questions.stem: Which statement about atom economy and waste in an industrial process is correct?

options.text: The higher the percentage yield, the higher the atom economy, so less waste is produced.
Atom economy counts one molecule of each substance, so the coefficients do not affect it.
A process with an atom economy of 100% produces no waste of any kind at all.
The lower the atom economy, the greater the proportion of reactant mass that becomes waste.

questions.explanation: The mass not in the desired product ends up in by-products, so atom economy and waste are inversely related.

questions.stem: A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. A student's titre is 12.50 cm³, found from two readings. What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?
Which reaction has an atom economy of 100% for the product named?

options.text: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), making calcium oxide
Any reaction that is carried out with a 100% yield

questions.explanation: This reaction has a single product, so every reactant atom ends up in it: 100%.

questions.stem: A student dissolves 2.5 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) in water and makes the solution up to 250.0 cm³. Which value of the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, is given to the appropriate number of significant figures?
questions.explanation: 2.5 ÷ 58.5 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.1709… The mass has only 2 significant figures, so the answer has 2: 0.17.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is manufactured by reacting methane with steam: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). In one batch, 16.0 kg of methane gave 4.80 kg of hydrogen. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen by this reaction? (Aᵣ: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0)
questions.explanation: 3 × 2.0 ÷ (16.0 + 18.0) × 100 = 6.0 ÷ 34.0 × 100 = 17.6%. The products total is the same: 28.0 + 6.0 = 34.0. The rest of the mass ends up as CO.

questions.stem: A student plots the volume of gas collected against time. The line of best fit is straight, but does not pass through the origin. It passes through (10 s, 14 cm³) and (50 s, 62 cm³). What is the gradient, in cm³ s⁻¹?
questions.explanation: (62 − 14) ÷ (50 − 10) = 48 ÷ 40 = 1.2. The line meets the y-axis at 2 cm³, so one point alone gives the wrong answer.

questions.stem: A student mixes two solutions in a polystyrene cup to find an enthalpy change. The thermometer has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C per reading, and the temperature rises by only about 4 °C. Which change would most reduce the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change, ΔT? -

options.text: Use larger volumes of the same two solutions.
Use more concentrated solutions, keeping the same volumes.
Start with both solutions at a higher temperature.
Record each temperature to two decimal places.

questions.explanation: More reacts in the same volume, so ΔT is larger (e.g. about 20 °C). The ±1.0 °C uncertainty in ΔT is then about 5% instead of 25%.
